notes.1: Some candidates offered fully correct solutions. Some other candidates were able to state the correct critical values but did not use them in a correct inequality. Candidates who drew a simple diagram to help them interpret the information in the question usually avoided this error. A few candidates multiplied out and then either factorised or used the formula. This was unnecessary and sometimes resulted in errors. A few candidates made sign errors when stating the critical values.
notes.2: – 2 The simplest method of solution was to start by writing the expression for y as 4 x – 5 x and then differentiate. This approach resulted in a much simpler derivative to be manipulated into the given form. Very few candidates chose this method. Those who did were often successful. The majority of candidates chose 3 – 2 to use the quotient rule, with a very small number applying the product rule to (4 x – 5) x . Candidates commonly made sign errors when forming the derivative using these methods as they were more complex. As the question required candidates to ‘show that’ the derivative could be written in a particular form, they needed to show sufficient detail in their working to justify their answer. For example, candidates using the quotient rule had to clearly demonstrate factorising or division in the final step. Most candidates who had formed a correct expression for the derivative were able to do this successfully.

notes.4: (a) In this question, candidates needed to explain why the function f could be formed by stating that the range of f was the same as its domain, or the equivalent. Very few candidates were able to offer an acceptable explanation. A few candidates offered incomplete explanations, such as ‘The domain is the set of real numbers’. Some candidates simply found, or attempted to find, an expression for f ( x ). (b) Most of the candidates who formed the correct expression for f ( x ) offered a fully correct graph with correct intercepts. A small number of these candidates incorrectly stated the value of one of the intercepts. A few others did not explicitly state one or both intercepts but marked unlabelled tick marks, to represent a scale, on each axis. This was not accepted as the question required that the intercepts be stated. Some candidates made no attempt to answer. (c) A small number of candidates offered fully correct solutions. A few candidates attempted to find the y - coordinates of the critical points, using x = – 1 and x = 3. This was creditable providing the expression used for f ( x ) had been found using a genuine attempt at a composite function. Some candidates went on to correctly interpret a as being the gradient of the line joining the two critical points. This was creditable, even if the coordinates had been found using (2 x – 1) for example, as it was a correct interpretation of what was required to solve the problem.
notes.key_messages: C andidates should read each question carefully and take notice of any key words or phrases. Candidates need to show sufficient method for marks to be awarded. When values have been found using incorrect expressions, for example, and the method used to find them is not s hown , credit is not given . For example, t he substitution of a value into a derivative should be shown so that the method can be seen and assessed. Candidates should check that their calculator is in the appropriate mode when working with trigonometric expressions, particularly in questions involving calculus or the solving of trigonometric equations . Candidates should also be aware of how to use their calculator to check their solutions. When a candidate rejects a solution it cannot be credited. Candidates should, therefore, think carefully before they decide to reject values they consider to be extraneous.

notes.9a: The simplest approach to solving this arithmetic progression problem was to find n by substituting the information given in the first three lines into the given formula . This could then be S = ( a + l ) used to find the value of d using the 31st term and the final steps of the problem were then accessible. A good number of candidates used this approach and offered fully correct solutions. A small number of candidates made an error in the final step, for example, prematurely rounding the value of 0.6875 when finding the final answer. Some candidates were able to find the value of n and/or d, but made no further progress. A few candidates found non - integer values for n . An alternative method of solution was to form the 31st term in terms of n and d then rearrange it to make n the subject. This could then be used to eliminate n from and solve for  18 + 30 d  = 2604 d . This was also fairly successful, although candidates who used this approach were more likely to make an error as the algebra was more complex.
notes.9bi: Candidates found this part of the question to be somewhat challenging. A few candidates were successful. It was essential to make a clear and precise statement to earn the mark available. notes.9bii: Candidates were more successful in this part of the question, although many still found it to be quite challenging. Many candidates earned the mark available for forming the correct expression for the sum to infinity. notes.10a: In this question, candidates first needed to find the unit vector in the direction given and then multiply by the speed of the particle, to find the velocity vector. This could then be used with the starting point given in the question, to form the position vector required. A few candidates carried out all of these steps correctly. A small number of candidates found the correct velocity vector but did not use it correctly. Some candidates were able to find the magnitude of the direction vector, but then combined this with the speed incorrectly, usually forming 10 i + 10.5 j as the velocity vector. Other candidates did not attempt to form the unit vector and simply used 58(20 i + 21 j ) as the velocity vector. Some final position vectors did not include t .
notes.10b: Candidates found this part of the question to be very challenging and many of them made no attempt to answer. Of those who did answer, a small proportion offered correct solutions. A few candidates attempted the direction vector but interchanged 7 and 24. A few other candidates found a value for the angle  but did not make any further, valid progress. notes.10c: In order to answer this part of the question, candidates needed to have two position vectors that included t . A completely correct solution depended on both the previous parts of the question being correct and, therefore, fully correct answers were not common. Partial credit was available to candidates forming appropriate equations using their position vectors providing they were of equivalent form. A small proportion of candidates equated the position vectors but did not equate the components of the vectors before making their decision.
